title: Splitting costs fairly with housemates
description: Shared houses run on shared money. A simple, agreed system for bills and basics prevents the small resentments that spoil good houses.

body.heading: Agree the system before the first bill
paragraphs: The conversation is easiest before any money is owed. Decide together: which costs are shared (rent, utilities, cleaning basics, shared staples like oil and foil), which are personal, and how the shared ones are divided — equally is usual, but rooms of very different sizes sometimes justify different shares.
Write it down, even in a shared note. Agreements made in good humour in September are hard to reconstruct from memory in February.

body.heading: One pot or an app, but one system
paragraphs: A shared kitty — a jar or account everyone pays a fixed amount into monthly — suits regular shared costs: when the bill arrives, the pot pays it, and nobody chases anybody. Splitting apps work well for irregular shared purchases, settling up in one transfer rather than twelve.
Whichever you choose, choose one. Money scattered across favours, loans, and half-remembered rounds is where housemate friction breeds.

body.heading: Handle problems early and lightly
paragraphs: If someone is struggling, a quiet word early is kinder than silence followed by an explosion. Most houses can flex for a month; what they cannot survive is surprise. Fairness maintained openly is a form of kindness, and good houses are worth the small awkwardness of talking about money plainly.
It helps to schedule a five-minute money chat once a term, before anything is wrong. Houses that talk about money routinely rarely have to talk about it urgently.

takeaway: Agree what is shared, how it is split, and which single system tracks it — before the first bill arrives, while everyone is still friends with the idea.
